questions.question: Star X has a radius three times that of star Y and a surface temperature half that of star Y. What is the luminosity of star X as a fraction of the luminosity of star Y? A 0.19, B 0.56, C 1.1, D 2.3
steps: Luminosity L = 4 pi r^2 sigma T^4, so L is proportional to r^2 T^4.
A uses r instead of r^2 (3/16), C uses r^2 T^3 (9/8) and D uses r^2 T^2 (9/4).

questions.question: Which row shows the later stages in the life of a star of similar mass to the Sun? A main sequence -> red supergiant -> supernova -> neutron star, B main sequence -> red giant -> supernova -> white dwarf, C main sequence -> red giant -> planetary nebula -> white dwarf, D main sequence -> white dwarf -> red giant -> planetary nebula
questions.answer: C: main sequence -> red giant -> planetary nebula -> white dwarf
steps: A star like the Sun leaves the main sequence when the core hydrogen is used up and becomes a red giant.
It then ejects its outer layers as a planetary nebula, and the remaining core becomes a white dwarf: option C.
A describes a much more massive star and B has a supernova for a star that is too light for one; D has the stages in the wrong order.

questions.question: Star Y has a surface temperature of 9800 K and a luminosity of 4.2 x 10^28 W. Calculate the radius of star Y. (Stefan-Boltzmann constant = 5.67 x 10^-8 W m^-2 K^-4.)
questions.answer: Radius = 2.5 x 10^9 m.
steps: Treat the star as a black body: L = 4 pi r^2 sigma T^4.
r = 2.53 x 10^9 m, which is 3.6 times the radius of the Sun.

questions.question: The parallax angle of a nearby star, measured from the Earth, is 0.042 arcseconds. Calculate the distance to the star in (i) parsecs and (ii) metres. (1 parsec = 3.09 x 10^16 m.)
steps: By the definition of the parsec, distance in parsecs d = 1 / p, with p in arcseconds.

questions.question: Explain why a star of much greater mass than the Sun ends its life in a supernova, whereas a star of similar mass to the Sun does not.
questions.answer: A massive star fuses elements up to iron, then its core collapses in a supernova; a Sun-like star becomes a white dwarf.
steps: In a very massive star gravity compresses the core to a much higher temperature, so successive fusion stages build heavier elements, up to iron
Iron has the highest binding energy per nucleon, so fusing iron absorbs energy rather than releasing it and the outward pressure from fusion stops
The core then collapses under gravity and the outer layers are thrown off in a supernova, leaving a neutron star or black hole
In a Sun-like star the core never becomes hot enough for the later stages of fusion; it expels its outer layers as a planetary nebula and the core remains as a white dwarf
accept: More massive stars have a greater gravitational pressure, so they reach higher core temperatures
A massive star fuses hydrogen much faster and so has a shorter life on the main sequence
The remnant becomes a neutron star or a black hole depending on the mass of the core
The star becomes a red supergiant, rather than a red giant, before the supernova

questions.question: Star P has a surface temperature of 3400 K and a luminosity 1.2 x 10^4 times that of the Sun. Calculate the wavelength at which star P emits radiation with maximum intensity. (Wien's displacement law constant = 2.898 x 10^-3 m K.)
questions.answer: Peak wavelength = 8.5 x 10^-7 m, in the infrared.
steps: Wien's law: lambda_max T = 2.898 x 10^-3 m K.
lambda_max = 2.898 x 10^-3 / 3400 = 8.52 x 10^-7 m (about 850 nm, which is in the infrared).

questions.question: Star P has a surface temperature of 3400 K and a luminosity 1.2 x 10^4 times that of the Sun. The luminosity of the Sun is 3.85 x 10^26 W. Calculate the radius of star P. (Stefan-Boltzmann constant = 5.67 x 10^-8 W m^-2 K^-4.)
questions.answer: Radius = 2.2 x 10^11 m.
steps: This is 320 times the Sun's radius of 6.96 x 10^8 m.

questions.question: Star P has a surface temperature of 3400 K and a luminosity 1.2 x 10^4 times that of the Sun. State where star P would be found on a Hertzsprung-Russell diagram and the type of star that it is.
questions.answer: Top right of the HR diagram (cool and very luminous): a red supergiant.
steps: Top right of the diagram: cool (3400 K) so to the right, and very luminous so near the top
It is a red supergiant (a star that has left the main sequence)
accept: Above and to the right of the main sequence
In the region of high luminosity and low surface temperature
It is a star in a late stage of its life that has expanded and cooled

questions.question: Star P has a surface temperature of 3400 K, lower than the Sun's temperature of 5800 K, but a luminosity 1.2 x 10^4 times that of the Sun. Explain how star P can be so much more luminous than the Sun, referring to the size of star P.
questions.answer: L is proportional to r^2 T^4: P is cooler, but its surface area is about 10^5 times larger.
steps: The luminosity is proportional to (surface area) x T^4, that is to r^2 T^4
The lower temperature reduces the power emitted per unit area by a factor of (3400 / 5800)^4 = 0.12 compared with the Sun
The radius of P is about 320 times that of the Sun, so its surface area is about 1 x 10^5 times larger, which outweighs the lower temperature
accept: L = 4 pi r^2 sigma T^4 with the ratio of luminosities worked out as (r / r_Sun)^2 (T / T_Sun)^4 = 1.2 x 10^4
Star P is a red supergiant: very large and cool
A much larger surface area means much more radiating surface, so more energy is emitted per second in total

questions.question: The cosmic microwave background radiation has the spectrum of a black body at a temperature of 2.7 K. (Wien's displacement law constant = 2.898 x 10^-3 m K.) At what wavelength does the radiation have its maximum intensity? A 7.8 x 10^-3 m, B 9.3 x 10^2 m, C 1.1 x 10^-6 m, D 1.1 x 10^-3 m
steps: Wien's law: lambda_max = 2.898 x 10^-3 / T = 2.898 x 10^-3 / 2.7 = 1.07 x 10^-3 m, in the microwave region (option D).
A multiplies the constant by T, B divides T by the constant (inverted), and C is a factor of 10^3 too small.

questions.question: A spectral line has a wavelength of 500 nm in the laboratory. In the light from a distant galaxy the same line is observed at a wavelength of 510 nm. What is the speed at which the galaxy is receding from the Earth? A 6.0 x 10^5 m s^-1, B 6.0 x 10^6 m s^-1, C 3.1 x 10^8 m s^-1, D 1.5 x 10^10 m s^-1
steps: For speeds much less than c, delta lambda / lambda = v / c, where lambda is the laboratory (emitted) wavelength.
A is a power of ten too small, C uses the ratio of the wavelengths (510 / 500) without subtracting 1, and D inverts the fractional change (500 / 10).

questions.question: The spectral lines in the light from distant galaxies are shifted towards longer wavelengths, and the shift is greater for galaxies that are further away. Explain what these observations suggest about the universe.
questions.answer: Galaxies recede faster the further away they are: the universe is expanding from an earlier hot, dense state.
steps: The longer observed wavelengths are a Doppler (red) shift, so the galaxies are receding from the Earth
The greater redshift of more distant galaxies shows that recession speed increases with distance (v proportional to d), as in a uniformly expanding universe
Tracing the expansion back in time, everything was once much closer together, supporting a Big Bang origin
accept: Space itself is expanding, so the wavelength of light is stretched as it travels
There is no centre of the expansion: every galaxy sees the others moving away
Hubble's law v = H0 d describes the relationship
The expansion can be used to estimate the age of the universe as 1 / H0

questions.question: Explain how the cosmic microwave background radiation provides evidence for the Big Bang model of the universe.
questions.answer: Uniform 2.7 K black-body radiation from all directions: the stretched remnant of the hot early universe.
steps: The radiation is detected from all directions with almost the same intensity, and has a black-body spectrum corresponding to a temperature of about 2.7 K
The Big Bang model predicts that the early universe was very hot and dense and filled with high-energy radiation, which should still be present as a background
As space expanded the wavelengths of this radiation were stretched (redshifted) into the microwave region, matching the observed spectrum
accept: The radiation is isotropic: the same from every direction, as expected if it fills the whole universe
The temperature of the radiation has fallen as the universe expanded
The peak wavelength of about 1 mm corresponds to a 2.7 K black body (Wien's law)

questions.question: State what is meant by a standard candle.
questions.answer: A source whose luminosity is known, so its distance can be found from the intensity measured at the Earth.
steps: A source (star or supernova) of known luminosity, which can be used to find distance from its measured intensity
accept: An object whose luminosity can be determined independently of its distance
An object of known power output (for example a Cepheid variable star or a supernova of a particular type)
An object whose intrinsic brightness is the same for all such objects

questions.question: A supernova, which is treated as a standard candle, has a peak luminosity of 1.0 x 10^36 W. The peak intensity of its light measured at the Earth is 1.0 x 10^-14 W m^-2. Calculate the distance to the supernova.
questions.answer: Distance = 2.8 x 10^24 m.
steps: Intensity I = L / (4 pi d^2), so d = sqrt(L / (4 pi I)).

questions.question: State Hubble's law.
questions.answer: The recession speed of a galaxy is directly proportional to its distance from the observer: v = H0 d.
steps: The recession speed of a galaxy is directly proportional to its distance from the observer
v = H0 d, where H0 is the Hubble constant
accept: The further away a galaxy is, the faster it is moving away from us
Redshift (z) is proportional to distance for nearby galaxies
The gradient of a graph of recession speed against distance is H0

questions.question: A spectral line from calcium has a wavelength of 393.4 nm in the laboratory. In light from a galaxy cluster the same line is observed at 401.7 nm. Calculate the speed at which the cluster is receding from the Earth.
questions.answer: Recession speed = 6.3 x 10^6 m s^-1.
steps: Redshift z = delta lambda / lambda = (401.7 - 393.4) / 393.4 = 0.0211.
For z much less than 1, v = z c.

questions.question: The galaxy cluster in (b) is receding at 6.33 x 10^6 m s^-1. Use Hubble's law with H0 = 2.3 x 10^-18 s^-1 to calculate the distance to the cluster in megaparsecs. (1 Mpc = 3.09 x 10^22 m.)
questions.answer: Distance = 89 Mpc.
steps: v = H0 d, so d = v / H0.

questions.question: Assuming that the galaxies have always moved apart at their present speeds, estimate the age of the universe in years from H0 = 2.3 x 10^-18 s^-1. (1 year = 3.15 x 10^7 s.)
steps: With constant speeds, the time since the galaxies were together is t = d / v = 1 / H0.

questions.question: Suggest two reasons why the actual age of the universe may differ from the value of 1 / H0.
questions.answer: The expansion rate has not been constant, and H0 is uncertain because galaxy distances are hard to measure.
steps: The expansion has not been at a constant rate (gravity slowed it in the past, and it may be accelerating now), so the galaxies have not always moved at their present speeds
There is uncertainty in H0, because the distances found using standard candles and other methods have uncertainties
accept: The galaxies also have random (peculiar) motions in addition to the expansion, which affects the measured speeds
The value of H0 depends on the sample of galaxies used and the calibration of the distance ladder
The Hubble constant itself has changed over time, so 1 / H0 only applies to the present rate of expansion
